study.title: Matthew 1 The genealogy and the birth of Jesus the Christ
study.overview: Matthew opens his gospel by showing that Jesus does not arise outside of the history of Israel, but as the fulfillment of the promises made to Abraham and David. Genealogy presents a real and theological line: God leads history through ordinary people, with faults, foreigners, crises and exile, until he reaches Joseph and Mary. Then the birth is narrated in order to affirm two central truths: Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit and was born of a virgin; and his name indicates his saving mission. The chapter concludes by confirming that Joseph obeyed the divine proclamation and that Jesus legally received the name given by God.

outline.title: The promised and organized lineage of Jesus
outline.explanation: Matthew presents Jesus as the son of David and the son of Abraham, linking him to the Messianic promises and blessing to the nations. The list is structured into three blocks of fourteen generations, passing through striking phases of Israel's history: patriarchs, monarchy and exile. The presence of women and morally complex moments shows that God's grace acts within a real, undepersonalized history.

outline.title: The virginal conception and the identity of the Savior
outline.explanation: Mary is found pregnant before the full marital union, and the text attributes conception to the Holy Spirit. Joseph, described as righteous, thinks of dissolving the engagement discreetly, but an angel guides him to receive Mary and to name the child Jesus. The birth is interpreted as prophetic fulfillment: Jesus will be the Savior of his people and Emmanuel, that is, God with us.

outline.title: The obedience of Joseph and the birth of Jesus
outline.explanation: Joseph responds to the dream with immediate obedience, receiving Mary and awaiting the birth. The text states that he had no marital relations with her until childbirth, reinforcing the unique origin of Jesus. At the end, Joseph gives the child the name Jesus, confirming his acceptance of the divine order and the mission of the child.

study.context: The chapter presents the origin of Jesus in the form of genealogy and birth narrative. The text itself highlights the connection with Abraham and David, the stage of Babylonian exile and the continuity of the lineage to Joseph. It is not necessary to assume additional details of date or place to realize the main goal: Matthew wants to prove, by Scripture and by the family history of Jesus, that he is the promised Christ.
study.theology: Matthew 1 teaches that the incarnation is the initiative of God and not a result of human action. The Holy Spirit is the agent of conception; therefore, Jesus is not only the human heir of David, but also the one whose origin is supernatural. Genealogy shows God's faithfulness to promises despite the sin and ruptures of the people. The inclusion of unexpected characters and the path through exile reveal grace, sovereignty and continuity of the covenant. The name Jesus summarizes the redemptive mission: to save his people from sins. The name Emmanuel adds the saving presence of God among his people. Joseph's obedience shows that true faith is expressed in concrete submission to the word received.

scholarViews.insight: Rahab's inclusion in the Messiah's lineage highlights the grace of God and shows that the text links genealogy to the Messianic identity of Jesus.
The gospel begins with the account of Christ's generation to show that he is really the promised Messiah, born of virgin and descendant of David.
The text on birth indicates that the human nature of Jesus was actually formed in the womb of the virgin by the power of the Holy Spirit.

questions: Why does Matthew organize the genealogy in three blocks of fourteen generations, and what does this emphasize about the history of Israel?
What does the expression Emanuel add to the idea that Jesus will save his people from sins?
What does Joseph's attitude teach about justice, mercy, and obedience when God's will seems to contradict human expectations?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader to trust that God rules history even when it goes through human faults, ruptures and waiting periods. He also invites to receive Jesus not only as a religious figure, but as the promised Savior and God present with us. In practice, this implies obeying the word of God with humility, like Joseph, and abandoning the attempt to completely control the ways of the Lord. Moreover, the presence of unlikely people in Jesus" lineage encourages the church to value the grace of God that reaches the unlikely and restores broken stories.
study.uncertainty: The chapter states that Joseph had no relations with Mary until the birth of Jesus, but the exact scope of the term translated "even" can be interpreted in different ways by the commentators. It is also not possible to determine, based only on this chapter and the notes provided, all historical details of the genealogy or fully reconcile the timelogical issues raised by some name lists. The confessional interpretations of Mary's perpetual virginity appear in the notes as opinion, not as a mandatory conclusion of the text.
